newsitem.title: UK: Labour, scenting power, opens pre-poll conference.
newsitem.headline: Labour, scenting power, opens pre-poll conference.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour Party opens its annual conference on Monday, hoping to woo an electorate weary of 17 years of Conservative rule with a political programme that is radical yet responsible.

Party leader Tony Blair, who holds a commanding 20-point lead in opinion polls, has sought to win the trust of floating voters who feel it is time for change but worry that "New" Labour" still harbours discredited tax-and-spend instincts.

Building on Blair's contention in a weekend interview that it would be "intellectually lazy" to gauge Labour's radicalism by its willingness to raise taxes, finance spokesman Gordon Brown will warn that the party cannot escape tough choices.
Brown will tell the conference, the last before general elections which must be held by May, that Labour must show an iron discipline in its approach to public spending.

The run-up to the conference has been marred by rumblings of discontent from left-wingers uneasy at what they see as Blair's eagerness to water down Labour's principles and loosen ties to the trade unions that founded the party a century ago.

But aides say Brown will argue that, by re-ordering its priorities, Labour is not jettisoning its ideals but making them possible. "Our prudence is not the abandonment of socialism, but the essence of it," he will say.

Labour is haunted by its candour at the 1992 election, when the Conservatives seized on its generous spending pledges to portray it as a party of crazed tax-raisers. Nervous voters decided to play safe and re-elected Prime Minister John Major.

The Labour leadership, determined not to offer similar openings in future, has headed off a call for a three billion pound ($4.7 billion) increase in basic pensions by referring the issue to a policy commission.
A former Labour cabinet minister, Baroness Barbara Castle, expressed dismay at the fudge. But Labour leaders, with a steely eye on the main prize of power, were unrepentant.

"What we are not going to do is promise more than we can deliver. That is painful, that is difficult, but what we have got to do is show the people of this country (they can) trust us," deputy leader John Prescott told BBC television.
Brown will also defend the move and argue that a Labour government will protect pensioners' standard of living by being tough on inflation.
He aims to please the party faithful by stressing Labour's commitment to shift resources from welfare to education as the key to tackling unemployment and job insecurity.
Aides say Brown will also reaffirm the determination of a Labour government to tackle youth unemployment by levying a windfall tax on the past profits of privatised utilities.
"They can lobby all they like. It will make no difference. I won't back down," Brown will say.
Blair, who staked out a claim in the weekend interview to what he called the "radical centre" of British politics, addresses the conference on Tuesday.
